sections.heading: A — Managing Time and Space
sections.markdown:
## A — Managing Time and Space
Authority: the Maine Bureau of Motor Vehicles presents this manual as preparation for safe vehicle operation and obtaining a driver license. [A06]
Source title: Maine Driver’s License Manual, issued under the Secretary of State. [A01]
Pinned edition: the frontmatter revision marker is Rev 4/24. [A02]
Selected path: first-time applicants studying the standard Class C license material; commercial endorsements are excluded. [A08]
Official question count remains unknown (verify ME-SEC08-COUNT); official passing standard remains unknown (verify ME-SEC08-PASS); official time limit remains unknown (verify ME-SEC08-TIME).
This dossier’s subject is Managing Time and Space; the source map controls coverage rather than an invented official exam weight.
Any quiz mastery target belongs to the accepted LearningLoop as product policy; it is not an official passing score.
The current issuer observation confirms this pinned document; an unknown legal effective date is retained in the registrar’s accepted disposition.

sections.heading: B — Managing Time and Space
sections.markdown:
## B — Managing Time and Space
Audience: English-language first-time standard-license applicants using the Managing Time and Space section.
Level: beginner study of the selected handbook material, followed by recall and application practice.
Prerequisite policy: understand the cited terminology before comparing exceptions; this is a teaching order, not an extra licensing eligibility requirement.
Coverage basis: the physical source range and the fact roster define this topic; no official topic percentage was supplied.

sections.heading: C — Managing Time and Space
sections.markdown:
## C — Managing Time and Space

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A75
Continually search ahead, beside and behind the vehicle, keeping the eyes moving rather than staring. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A75
Early hazard detection creates time to change speed or direction. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A75
The driver must have a clear view through all windows, windshield and mirrors. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A75
Keep the windshield clean, stop to clean it when necessary and maintain a full washer reservoir. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A75
Smoking creates a film inside the windows, so clean the interior glass frequently if you smoke. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A75
Before driving, remove snow, frost and ice from every window and from headlamps and taillamps. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A75
Do not hang mirror objects or place windshield decals where they block the driver’s view. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A75
If the license requires corrective lenses, wear them whenever driving. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A75
Keep spare glasses in the vehicle in case the regular pair is lost or damaged. [A75]
Source: [A75 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A76
Look well ahead to plan the path, leaving space behind large vehicles that would block the view. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A76
The manual recommends scanning 20 to 30 seconds ahead, taking in the whole scene rather than only the road center. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A76
Include roadside people, vehicles, warning and direction signs, and animals in the forward search. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A76
If you see a deer, use the horn and look for others following it. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A76
A person entering a parked car can warn that a door may reopen or the car may move into the lane. [A76]
Source: [A76 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A77
Look especially to the sides near busy shopping or parking areas, construction, sidewalks, schools, parks and sales. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A77
The illustrated school-crossing warning has a five-sided pedestrian symbol above a directional arrow. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A77
The signed school-zone guidance sets 15 miles per hour during recess, when children arrive or leave during opening or closing hours, or when school-speed lights flash during those hours. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A77
Approach tracks looking both ways and anticipate vehicles such as buses and tank trucks that must stop. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A77
In heavy traffic, wait before the railroad tracks rather than stopping on them. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A77
Slow and check both directions at a railroad crossing even if its warning light is not flashing, since the equipment may not be working. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A77
Flashing railroad red lights require a stop at least 15 feet from the crossing. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A77
Never drive around a railroad gate or barrier. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A77
At multiple tracks, wait after a train passes until both directions are visible because another train may approach. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A77
Do not shift a manual transmission while crossing railroad tracks. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A77
An Exempt track sign does not guarantee that the track is unused; check for trains there too. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A77
Check the rear mirror every 6 to 8 seconds to track following traffic and rear space. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A77
Check behind when changing lanes, slowing, stopping or before entering an intersection. [A77]
Source: [A77 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A78
Check behind before backing or descending a long or steep hill, and look briefly in the mirrors before a sudden slowdown. [A78]
Source: [A78 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A78
Before slowing for a hidden hazard, a side-road turn, parking or pedestrians, check whether following traffic can react. [A78]
Source: [A78 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A78
Allow extra space around drivers whose views are blocked, who are reversing or whose windows are obscured by snow or ice. [A78]
Source: [A78 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A78
Give extra space to potentially distracted delivery or construction workers and children who may enter the road. [A78]
Source: [A78 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A79
Expect sudden moves from confused tourists or drivers slowing without an obvious reason. [A79]
Source: [A79 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A79
If a driver overtakes toward a curve or oncoming traffic, slow and allow the vehicle back into your lane. [A79]
Source: [A79 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec08-F34 | anchor: A79
If another driver may be forced into your lane by an obstruction or road user, slow and move right as far as practical. [A79]
Source: [A79 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec08-F35 | anchor: A79
Safe speed depends on road and traffic conditions, the speed limit and a safe following distance. [A79]
Source: [A79 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec08-F36 | anchor: A79
On a long or steep uphill approach, check mirrors early for trucks or buses building speed. [A79]
Source: [A79 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec08-F37 | anchor: A80
Slow before a curve and choose a speed that permits slight acceleration through it. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F38 | anchor: A80
Slow further in a curve when grip is poor, another vehicle is ahead or the curve’s end is not visible. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

Misconceptions: a posted limit is a maximum rather than a compulsory speed. [A81]
Mnemonic: scan, leave room, adapt speed, communicate.
Glossary: a search pattern checks ahead, beside and behind. [A75]
Dynamic facts: stopping illustrations and ambiguous rail/school wording remain source debt.

sections.heading: C — Managing Time and Space
sections.markdown:
## C — Managing Time and Space

FACT_ID: sec08-F39 | anchor: A80
Hard braking in a curve, excessive speed or a very sharp curve can cause loss of tire grip and a skid. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F40 | anchor: A80
The illustrated angular left arrow warns of a sharp left curve, while the curved right arrow warns of a right curve. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F41 | anchor: A80
Reduce speed at the first signs of rain, snow, sleet or ice because slippery roads increase stopping and steering difficulty. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F42 | anchor: A80
The manual’s wet-road guideline is a speed reduction of 5 to 10 miles per hour. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F43 | anchor: A80
For packed snow, the guidance is to reduce to half the dry-road speed; on ice, slow to a crawl. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F44 | anchor: A80
Wet leaves, gravel and falling or drifting snow can make a road slippery. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F45 | anchor: A80
At the start of rain, road oil can create particularly slippery pavement until it washes away. [A80]
Source: [A80 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec08-F46 | anchor: A81
On cold wet days, bridges and overpasses tend to freeze first and dry last. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F47 | anchor: A81
Road ice near freezing can be wetter and more slippery than at colder temperatures. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F48 | anchor: A81
Hydroplaning occurs when tires ride on a water film rather than maintaining road contact. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F49 | anchor: A81
Heavy rain and high speed can eliminate tire contact, with worn tires doing so at lower speeds. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F50 | anchor: A81
To reduce hydroplaning risk, keep tires in good condition and slow on wet roads. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F51 | anchor: A81
Do not drive into a large body of standing water; use another route if the road is flooded. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F52 | anchor: A81
Total stopping distance extends from recognizing the need to stop until the vehicle is fully stopped. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F53 | anchor: A81
Higher speed increases the time and distance needed to stop. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F54 | anchor: A81
Perception time is the interval needed to recognize that stopping is necessary; the manual gives an alert-driver average of three-quarters to 1 second. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F55 | anchor: A81
Reaction time covers moving from accelerator to brake and starting braking; the manual gives an average of three-quarters to 1 second. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F56 | anchor: A81
Braking distance is the vehicle’s stopping travel once braking occurs. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F57 | anchor: A81
A posted speed is a maximum rather than a required driving speed; slow further when road or weather conditions make it unsafe. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F58 | anchor: A81
Unless a sign states otherwise, the listed Maine maximum outside business, residential or built-up areas is 45 miles per hour. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F59 | anchor: A81
Unless posted otherwise, the listed maximum in a business, residential or built-up district is 25 miles per hour. [A81]
Source: [A81 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec08-F60 | anchor: A82
Exceeding a posted school-zone limit brings twice the usual speeding fine. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec08-F61 | anchor: A82
Exceeding a posted speed limit, highway racing and reckless driving are prohibited. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec08-F62 | anchor: A82
Do not obstruct normal reasonable traffic by driving too slowly unless a lower speed is needed for safety. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec08-F63 | anchor: A82
Some highways post minimum speeds. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec08-F64 | anchor: A82
Tire and road condition determine available grip, so replace tires before the tread becomes unsafe. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec08-F65 | anchor: A82
At night, keep speed low enough to stop within the illuminated distance you can actually see. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec08-F66 | anchor: A82
If heavy rain, snow or dense fog prevents adequate vision even at low speed, leave the road and wait for improvement. [A82]
Source: [A82 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec08-F67 | anchor: A83
Approach a blind intersection slowly enough to stop for a vehicle emerging from behind an obstruction. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F68 | anchor: A83
Slow before a steep hill or sharp curve so you can stop for a hazard beyond it. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F69 | anchor: A83
Allow space beside parked vehicles and be ready to stop for doors or people emerging between them. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F70 | anchor: A83
Heavy traffic reduces available space and reaction room, requiring a lower speed. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F71 | anchor: A83
Reduce speed in busy shopping or downtown areas, narrow bridges or tunnels, toll plazas and places with schools or playgrounds. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F72 | anchor: A83
Repeatedly passing slower traffic increases opportunities for conflict even when your own speed remains within the limit. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F73 | anchor: A83
If many cars are trying to pass, permit safe passing by easing speed or pulling right rather than forcing traffic to bunch behind. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F74 | anchor: A83
For freeway entry, find a gap and accelerate in the entrance lane to merge smoothly at highway traffic speed. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec08-F75 | anchor: A83
On an expressway exit, do not decelerate until reaching the exit lane. [A83]
Source: [A83 -> pdf-0083]

sections.heading: C2 — Managing Time and Space
sections.markdown:
## C2 — Managing Time and Space

FACT_ID: sec08-R01 | anchor: A84
Adjust speed early when approaching a slow-moving vehicle, especially one losing speed uphill or taking longer to accelerate. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R02 | anchor: A84
A red-bordered orange triangle identifies the slow-moving vehicles described, which usually travel at 25 miles per hour or less. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R03 | anchor: A84
Warning signs call for reducing speed to allow time to react to the hazard ahead. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R04 | anchor: A84
The pictured traffic-light warning is a yellow diamond containing the red-yellow-green signal image. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R05 | anchor: A84
The pictured merging warning shows a right branch joining the through lane ahead. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R06 | anchor: A84
Opposing vertical arrows on a yellow diamond warn of two-way traffic. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R07 | anchor: A84
The divided-highway-ends picture warns that the central separation ends ahead. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R08 | anchor: A84
The divided-highway-begins picture warns of a central separation starting ahead. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R09 | anchor: A84
A deer silhouette on a yellow diamond warns of a deer-crossing area. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R10 | anchor: A84
The illustrated right-lane-end warning directs traffic to merge left. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R11 | anchor: A84
The bicycle warning calls for extra attention to bicycles or a bicycle crossing. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R12 | anchor: A84
The illustrated cross-shaped symbol warns of an intersection ahead. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R13 | anchor: A84
The upward arrow above a stop-sign symbol warns that a stop sign is ahead. [A84]
Source: [A84 -> pdf-0084]

FACT_ID: sec08-R14 | anchor: A85
A space cushion is room around the vehicle that provides more reaction time. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec08-R15 | anchor: A85
Maintain space on all sides according to speed and road conditions. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec08-R16 | anchor: A85
The basic following interval is at least 4 seconds, with extra space needed in adverse conditions. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec08-R17 | anchor: A85
Measure a following gap from when the leading vehicle’s rear passes a fixed point until your vehicle reaches it. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec08-R18 | anchor: A85
If you reach that point before 4 seconds have elapsed, slow and recheck until the gap is at least 4 seconds. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec08-R19 | anchor: A85
Increase following distance on slippery roads and behind bicycles or motorcycles, especially where a rider may fall. [A85]
Source: [A85 -> pdf-0085]

FACT_ID: sec08-R20 | anchor: A86
Ease speed slightly to help a following driver complete a pass. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec08-R21 | anchor: A86
Leave more following space behind a large vehicle or trailer when its driver’s rear view or your forward view is restricted. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec08-R22 | anchor: A86
Do not pass a large vehicle on the right when it may be preparing a wide right turn. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec08-R23 | anchor: A86
Consider large vehicles’ downhill momentum and uphill speed loss when deciding whether to pass them. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec08-R24 | anchor: A86
When stopped behind a truck or bus, leave rollback space, especially on a hill. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec08-R25 | anchor: A86
Increase the following gap at night, in fog or bad weather, at high speed, with a heavy load or while towing. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec08-R26 | anchor: A86
Expect school buses and flammable-liquid tank trucks to stop at railroad crossings and slow early to leave stopping room. [A86]
Source: [A86 -> pdf-0086]

FACT_ID: sec08-R27 | anchor: A87
Avoid staying alongside another vehicle; pull ahead or fall back to preserve side space and avoid its blind spot. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec08-R28 | anchor: A87
Keep space from oncoming traffic and avoid crowding the center line. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec08-R29 | anchor: A87
Give entering traffic room by changing lanes or slowing when feasible. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec08-R30 | anchor: A87
Avoid driving beside other vehicles near freeway exits because they may suddenly exit or return to the freeway. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec08-R31 | anchor: A87
Leave side space beside parked cars and extra room for pedestrians, children and cyclists. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec08-R32 | anchor: A87
When a tractor-trailer passes you, move toward the right side of your lane to increase separation. [A87]
Source: [A87 -> pdf-0087]

FACT_ID: sec08-R33 | anchor: A88
Create extra following distance before slowing or turning, and help rear traffic by keeping a steady speed and signaling early. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec08-R34 | anchor: A88
If a tailgater can pass in a lane to your right, move right to facilitate the pass. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec08-R35 | anchor: A88
Without a right lane, wait for a clear route ahead and reduce speed gradually to encourage the tailgater to pass. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec08-R36 | anchor: A88
With parked cars on the right and oncoming cars on the left, choose a middle path that balances the hazards. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec08-R37 | anchor: A88
When a cyclist and an oncoming car would squeeze the same gap, slow and let the car pass before overtaking the cyclist with 3 feet of room. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> pdf-0088]

sections.heading: C2 — Managing Time and Space
sections.markdown:
## C2 — Managing Time and Space

FACT_ID: sec08-R38 | anchor: A88
When merging, crossing or entering existing traffic, yield and allow enough room to avoid interfering with vehicles already there. [A88]
Source: [A88 -> pdf-0088]

FACT_ID: sec08-R39 | anchor: A89
The manual calls for a 4-second merging gap for lane changes, freeway entry and road merges. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R40 | anchor: A89
Do not squeeze into an undersized gap; leave an adequate space cushion. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R41 | anchor: A89
Cross multiple lanes one at a time rather than stopping to wait for every lane to clear at once. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R42 | anchor: A89
The from-stop crossing examples call for about half a city block or a full highway block of gap. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R43 | anchor: A89
For turning into existing traffic, the examples allow about two-thirds of a city block or 2 highway blocks to turn and accelerate. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R44 | anchor: A89
Cross traffic only with room to finish; a halfway stop is safe only if a median is large enough to contain the vehicle. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R45 | anchor: A89
Do not enter an intersection, even on green, if vehicles or people block the onward path. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R46 | anchor: A89
Do not rely solely on another driver’s turn signal; wait until the turn begins before acting on it. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R47 | anchor: A89
Headlights improve the vehicle’s visibility to other road users during daylight as well as at night. [A89]
Source: [A89 -> pdf-0089]

FACT_ID: sec08-R48 | anchor: A90
Use headlights when visibility is too dim to see 1,000 feet ahead or when the windshield wipers run continuously. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R49 | anchor: A90
Maine requires headlights while driving from sunset through sunrise. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R50 | anchor: A90
Use headlights when driving away from a rising or setting sun and whenever seeing other vehicles becomes difficult. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R51 | anchor: A90
Do not substitute parking lights alone when headlights are needed. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R52 | anchor: A90
Use high beams when possible, particularly on unfamiliar roads, in construction areas or near roadside people. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R53 | anchor: A90
For a multiple-beam vehicle, dim or select low beam within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or when following within 300 feet, and switch off an auxiliary fog light. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R54 | anchor: A90
Use low beams in fog, snow or heavy rain to avoid reflected high-beam glare. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R55 | anchor: A90
If an oncoming driver fails to dim high beams, slow and look toward the right road edge; do not retaliate with your own bright beams. [A90]
Source: [A90 -> pdf-0090]

FACT_ID: sec08-R56 | anchor: A91
Use the horn for a needed collision-prevention warning, not without cause or merely to make loud noise. [A91]
Source: [A91 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec08-R57 | anchor: A91
A light early horn tap can warn a pedestrian or cyclist entering the lane, a driver turning into your lane or someone who has not seen you. [A91]
Source: [A91 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec08-R58 | anchor: A91
Avoid startling cyclists or horses with the horn, but use a sharp warning when danger is near. [A91]
Source: [A91 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec08-R59 | anchor: A91
Signal before changing lanes, turning, merging, entering or leaving a freeway or parking lot, or turning into a driveway. [A91]
Source: [A91 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec08-R60 | anchor: A91
Tap the brake to warn of a slowdown for a turn without a separate exit lane or for parking or turning before an intersection. [A91]
Source: [A91 -> pdf-0091]

FACT_ID: sec08-R61 | anchor: A92
Signal even if no other road user is visible, and signal early enough to allow at least 100 feet before a turn or change. [A92]
Source: [A92 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec08-R62 | anchor: A92

sections.heading: D — Managing Time and Space
sections.markdown:
## D — Managing Time and Space
Accuracy scope: Managing Time and Space facts use the pinned official PDF and one physical page per fact; original phrasing preserves actor qualifications, exceptions and modal verbs.
The narrative braking example and stopping table use incompatible figures at the same example speed; no table-row stopping answer is exported until assumptions are reconciled. Official table pixels were inspected. [A81] [A82]
The rail-release sentence offers seeing a clear route as an alternative to waiting for flashing lights to stop; that alternative is not promoted to a stable permission to cross an active warning. [A77]
The printed half-hour opening/closing definition needs clarification before being represented as precise school clock windows. The explicit recess/children/flashing-sign triggers are preserved. [A77]
The cold-day washer prohibition does not distinguish fluid ratings; its vehicle-specific scope is held for clarification. [A75]
Fixed vehicle mass, tire-contact area, headlight-range/speed illustrations and high/low-beam distance multipliers lack sufficient vehicle assumptions for universal learner claims. [A80] [A82] [A90]
Approximate block-length entry gaps are source examples, not fixed distances or assurances independent of conditions. [A89]
The warning-sign and hand-signal pictures were inspected; meanings are not inferred from extracted labels alone. The stopping table is not copied into a learner table. [A84] [A92]
The source’s idealized same-speed collision-immunity sentence is not treated as a guarantee, and the cross-page low-turn-speed phrase is not taught as a compulsory minimum. [A83]
Motorcycle-only equipment requirements and large-commercial emergency-device placement are outside this standard-passenger-car scope. [A90] [A92]
Confidence process: every drafted fact received a same-model source-context check before submission; independent coverage and hallucination QA remain pending.
Officeholders, telephone numbers and changing administrative details are excluded from stable learner statements. No source attribution is a legal or clinical signoff.

ranked.label: Continually search ahead, beside and behind the vehicle, keeping the eyes moving rather than staring.
Early hazard detection creates time to change speed or direction.
The driver must have a clear view through all windows, windshield and mirrors.
Keep the windshield clean, stop to clean it when necessary and maintain a full washer reservoir.
Smoking creates a film inside the windows, so clean the interior glass frequently if you smoke.
Before driving, remove snow, frost and ice from every window and from headlamps and taillamps.
Do not hang mirror objects or place windshield decals where they block the driver’s view.
If the license requires corrective lenses, wear them whenever driving.
Keep spare glasses in the vehicle in case the regular pair is lost or damaged.
Look well ahead to plan the path, leaving space behind large vehicles that would block the view.
The manual recommends scanning 20 to 30 seconds ahead, taking in the whole scene rather than only the road center.
Include roadside people, vehicles, warning and direction signs, and animals in the forward search.
If you see a deer, use the horn and look for others following it.
A person entering a parked car can warn that a door may reopen or the car may move into the lane.
Look especially to the sides near busy shopping or parking areas, construction, sidewalks, schools, parks and sales.
The illustrated school-crossing warning has a five-sided pedestrian symbol above a directional arrow.
The signed school-zone guidance sets 15 miles per hour during recess, when children arrive or leave during opening or closing hours, or when school-speed lights flash during those hours.
Approach tracks looking both ways and anticipate vehicles such as buses and tank trucks that must stop.
In heavy traffic, wait before the railroad tracks rather than stopping on them.
Slow and check both directions at a railroad crossing even if its warning light is not flashing, since the equipment may not be working.
Flashing railroad red lights require a stop at least 15 feet from the crossing.
Never drive around a railroad gate or barrier.
At multiple tracks, wait after a train passes until both directions are visible because another train may approach.
Do not shift a manual transmission while crossing railroad tracks.
An Exempt track sign does not guarantee that the track is unused; check for trains there too.
Check the rear mirror every 6 to 8 seconds to track following traffic and rear space.
Check behind when changing lanes, slowing, stopping or before entering an intersection.
Check behind before backing or descending a long or steep hill, and look briefly in the mirrors before a sudden slowdown.
Before slowing for a hidden hazard, a side-road turn, parking or pedestrians, check whether following traffic can react.
Allow extra space around drivers whose views are blocked, who are reversing or whose windows are obscured by snow or ice.
Give extra space to potentially distracted delivery or construction workers and children who may enter the road.
Expect sudden moves from confused tourists or drivers slowing without an obvious reason.
If a driver overtakes toward a curve or oncoming traffic, slow and allow the vehicle back into your lane.
If another driver may be forced into your lane by an obstruction or road user, slow and move right as far as practical.
Safe speed depends on road and traffic conditions, the speed limit and a safe following distance.
On a long or steep uphill approach, check mirrors early for trucks or buses building speed.
Slow before a curve and choose a speed that permits slight acceleration through it.
Slow further in a curve when grip is poor, another vehicle is ahead or the curve’s end is not visible.
Hard braking in a curve, excessive speed or a very sharp curve can cause loss of tire grip and a skid.
The illustrated angular left arrow warns of a sharp left curve, while the curved right arrow warns of a right curve.
Reduce speed at the first signs of rain, snow, sleet or ice because slippery roads increase stopping and steering difficulty.
The manual’s wet-road guideline is a speed reduction of 5 to 10 miles per hour.
For packed snow, the guidance is to reduce to half the dry-road speed; on ice, slow to a crawl.
Wet leaves, gravel and falling or drifting snow can make a road slippery.
At the start of rain, road oil can create particularly slippery pavement until it washes away.
On cold wet days, bridges and overpasses tend to freeze first and dry last.
Road ice near freezing can be wetter and more slippery than at colder temperatures.
Hydroplaning occurs when tires ride on a water film rather than maintaining road contact.
Heavy rain and high speed can eliminate tire contact, with worn tires doing so at lower speeds.
To reduce hydroplaning risk, keep tires in good condition and slow on wet roads.
Do not drive into a large body of standing water; use another route if the road is flooded.
Total stopping distance extends from recognizing the need to stop until the vehicle is fully stopped.
Higher speed increases the time and distance needed to stop.
Perception time is the interval needed to recognize that stopping is necessary; the manual gives an alert-driver average of three-quarters to 1 second.
Reaction time covers moving from accelerator to brake and starting braking; the manual gives an average of three-quarters to 1 second.
Braking distance is the vehicle’s stopping travel once braking occurs.
A posted speed is a maximum rather than a required driving speed; slow further when road or weather conditions make it unsafe.
Unless a sign states otherwise, the listed Maine maximum outside business, residential or built-up areas is 45 miles per hour.
Unless posted otherwise, the listed maximum in a business, residential or built-up district is 25 miles per hour.
Exceeding a posted school-zone limit brings twice the usual speeding fine.
Exceeding a posted speed limit, highway racing and reckless driving are prohibited.
Do not obstruct normal reasonable traffic by driving too slowly unless a lower speed is needed for safety.
Some highways post minimum speeds.
Tire and road condition determine available grip, so replace tires before the tread becomes unsafe.
At night, keep speed low enough to stop within the illuminated distance you can actually see.
If heavy rain, snow or dense fog prevents adequate vision even at low speed, leave the road and wait for improvement.
Approach a blind intersection slowly enough to stop for a vehicle emerging from behind an obstruction.
Slow before a steep hill or sharp curve so you can stop for a hazard beyond it.
Allow space beside parked vehicles and be ready to stop for doors or people emerging between them.
Heavy traffic reduces available space and reaction room, requiring a lower speed.
Reduce speed in busy shopping or downtown areas, narrow bridges or tunnels, toll plazas and places with schools or playgrounds.
Repeatedly passing slower traffic increases opportunities for conflict even when your own speed remains within the limit.
If many cars are trying to pass, permit safe passing by easing speed or pulling right rather than forcing traffic to bunch behind.
For freeway entry, find a gap and accelerate in the entrance lane to merge smoothly at highway traffic speed.
On an expressway exit, do not decelerate until reaching the exit lane.
Adjust speed early when approaching a slow-moving vehicle, especially one losing speed uphill or taking longer to accelerate.
A red-bordered orange triangle identifies the slow-moving vehicles described, which usually travel at 25 miles per hour or less.
Warning signs call for reducing speed to allow time to react to the hazard ahead.
The pictured traffic-light warning is a yellow diamond containing the red-yellow-green signal image.
The pictured merging warning shows a right branch joining the through lane ahead.
Opposing vertical arrows on a yellow diamond warn of two-way traffic.
The divided-highway-ends picture warns that the central separation ends ahead.
The divided-highway-begins picture warns of a central separation starting ahead.
A deer silhouette on a yellow diamond warns of a deer-crossing area.
The illustrated right-lane-end warning directs traffic to merge left.
The bicycle warning calls for extra attention to bicycles or a bicycle crossing.
The illustrated cross-shaped symbol warns of an intersection ahead.
The upward arrow above a stop-sign symbol warns that a stop sign is ahead.
A space cushion is room around the vehicle that provides more reaction time.
Maintain space on all sides according to speed and road conditions.
The basic following interval is at least 4 seconds, with extra space needed in adverse conditions.
Measure a following gap from when the leading vehicle’s rear passes a fixed point until your vehicle reaches it.
If you reach that point before 4 seconds have elapsed, slow and recheck until the gap is at least 4 seconds.
Increase following distance on slippery roads and behind bicycles or motorcycles, especially where a rider may fall.
Ease speed slightly to help a following driver complete a pass.
Leave more following space behind a large vehicle or trailer when its driver’s rear view or your forward view is restricted.
Do not pass a large vehicle on the right when it may be preparing a wide right turn.
Consider large vehicles’ downhill momentum and uphill speed loss when deciding whether to pass them.
When stopped behind a truck or bus, leave rollback space, especially on a hill.
Increase the following gap at night, in fog or bad weather, at high speed, with a heavy load or while towing.
Expect school buses and flammable-liquid tank trucks to stop at railroad crossings and slow early to leave stopping room.
Avoid staying alongside another vehicle; pull ahead or fall back to preserve side space and avoid its blind spot.
Keep space from oncoming traffic and avoid crowding the center line.
Give entering traffic room by changing lanes or slowing when feasible.
Avoid driving beside other vehicles near freeway exits because they may suddenly exit or return to the freeway.
Leave side space beside parked cars and extra room for pedestrians, children and cyclists.
When a tractor-trailer passes you, move toward the right side of your lane to increase separation.
Create extra following distance before slowing or turning, and help rear traffic by keeping a steady speed and signaling early.
If a tailgater can pass in a lane to your right, move right to facilitate the pass.
Without a right lane, wait for a clear route ahead and reduce speed gradually to encourage the tailgater to pass.
With parked cars on the right and oncoming cars on the left, choose a middle path that balances the hazards.
When a cyclist and an oncoming car would squeeze the same gap, slow and let the car pass before overtaking the cyclist with 3 feet of room.
When merging, crossing or entering existing traffic, yield and allow enough room to avoid interfering with vehicles already there.
The manual calls for a 4-second merging gap for lane changes, freeway entry and road merges.
Do not squeeze into an undersized gap; leave an adequate space cushion.
Cross multiple lanes one at a time rather than stopping to wait for every lane to clear at once.
The from-stop crossing examples call for about half a city block or a full highway block of gap.
For turning into existing traffic, the examples allow about two-thirds of a city block or 2 highway blocks to turn and accelerate.
Cross traffic only with room to finish; a halfway stop is safe only if a median is large enough to contain the vehicle.
Do not enter an intersection, even on green, if vehicles or people block the onward path.
Do not rely solely on another driver’s turn signal; wait until the turn begins before acting on it.
Headlights improve the vehicle’s visibility to other road users during daylight as well as at night.
Use headlights when visibility is too dim to see 1,000 feet ahead or when the windshield wipers run continuously.
Maine requires headlights while driving from sunset through sunrise.
Use headlights when driving away from a rising or setting sun and whenever seeing other vehicles becomes difficult.
Do not substitute parking lights alone when headlights are needed.
Use high beams when possible, particularly on unfamiliar roads, in construction areas or near roadside people.
For a multiple-beam vehicle, dim or select low beam within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or when following within 300 feet, and switch off an auxiliary fog light.
Use low beams in fog, snow or heavy rain to avoid reflected high-beam glare.
If an oncoming driver fails to dim high beams, slow and look toward the right road edge; do not retaliate with your own bright beams.
Use the horn for a needed collision-prevention warning, not without cause or merely to make loud noise.
A light early horn tap can warn a pedestrian or cyclist entering the lane, a driver turning into your lane or someone who has not seen you.
Avoid startling cyclists or horses with the horn, but use a sharp warning when danger is near.
Signal before changing lanes, turning, merging, entering or leaving a freeway or parking lot, or turning into a driveway.
Tap the brake to warn of a slowdown for a turn without a separate exit lane or for parking or turning before an intersection.
Signal even if no other road user is visible, and signal early enough to allow at least 100 feet before a turn or change.
Use hand signals when the electrical turn signals fail.
When the intended turn lies beyond an intersection, delay the signal until after passing that intersection.
After a turn or lane change, make sure the signal cancels.
A driver’s left arm held straight out horizontally signals a left turn.
A driver’s left arm bent upward signals a right turn.
A driver’s left arm bent downward signals slowing or stopping.
For a roadside breakdown, pull completely out of traffic if possible and use emergency flashers, or the appropriate turn signal if there are no flashers.
Raise the hood to indicate an emergency and stop where approaching drivers can see the vehicle, avoiding blind hilltops or curves.
If emergency flares are available, place them at least 100 feet behind the stopped car.
Without flares, remain off the roadway and use a cloth or flag if available to warn approaching traffic.
Do not change a tire if it would require standing in a traffic lane.
Drive where others can see you and avoid remaining beside and slightly behind another vehicle.
Move ahead or fall back to leave another driver’s blind spot, and pass through it promptly when overtaking.
